cur:manuscripts2-utrecht-psalm-89-christ.summary: The cross-nimbed Christ-Logos, holding a cross-staff, spear and shield, stands within a mandorla among angels with the sun and moon of morning and evening, and stands guard over a walled enclosure containing a tabernacle: 'Lord, thou hast been our dwelling place in all generations'. Outside sits Terra holding a globe, and men are mown down like grass. The psalm on the brevity of life is set beneath an eternal protector.
facts: The Utrecht Psalter illustrates every psalm and canticle with a lively pen drawing — 166 in all — that translates the words of the text, often literally, into images; in these the Lord of the psalms is regularly shown as the youthful Christ-Logos.
The psalter was made in or near Reims, probably under Archbishop Ebbo (816–835); some scholars argue for a date around 850 under his successor Hincmar.
cur:manuscripts2-utrecht-psalm-89-christ.notes: The figure of the Lord is identified as Christ (the Christ-Logos) following the commentary of the Utrecht University Library's annotated edition, which describes the psalter's consistent practice of drawing the God of the psalms as the youthful Christ. The image is a crop of the drawing from the library's IIIF image server.

cur:objects2-seal-paul-seleucia.summary: On this seal the Theotokos appears as a frontal bust holding before her breast a medallion containing the bust of the Christ Child, flanked by cruciform monograms; the reverse invokes her help for 'your servant Paul, metropolitan of Seleucia'. The image of Christ shown within a clipeus held by his Mother is an early form of the type later called the Virgin Nikopoios or Blachernitissa.
facts: The circular legend on the reverse reads, in Greek, 'Theotokos, help your servant', a formula found on countless Byzantine seals.
Seals of this kind were attached by cords to letters and documents to authenticate them and keep them closed.
cur:objects2-seal-paul-seleucia.notes: Numismatic-trade specimen photographed by CNG; the iconographic label 'Nikopoios/Blachernitissa' is a later art-historical term.
